items: Explain Event-Driven Architecture (EDA) and its benefits for decoupling producers and consumers.
Separate the read and write models using CQRS and know when it pays off.
Describe Event Sourcing and how it differs from storing current state.
Apply the Hexagonal (ports & adapters) pattern to isolate domain logic from infrastructure.
Event-Driven Architecture (EDA) — components communicate by emitting and reacting to events rather than direct calls.
CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) — splitting write (command) and read (query) sides, possibly with different models.
Event Sourcing — persisting state as an append-only log of events; current state is a replay/Projection.
Aggregate (in ES) — rebuilt by replaying its event stream from the beginning or from a snapshot.
Hexagonal Architecture — domain core surrounded by ports (interfaces) and adapters (infrastructure implementations).
Port — an interface the domain exposes or requires. Adapter — a concrete technology binding for a port.

blocks.text: In EDA, a service emits a fact that happened ("OrderPlaced") to a broker (Kafka, RabbitMQ, Pulsar). Other services subscribe and react, without the producer knowing who they are. This inverts the dependency: producers are decoupled from consumers, new subscribers can be added without touching the producer, and the system absorbs load spikes via buffered queues. The cost is eventual consistency and the need for good tooling to trace and replay event flows.

A single model optimized for both writes (enforce invariants, validate) and reads (dashboards, joins, projections) is often a compromise that serves neither well. CQRS separates them: the command side processes intent and updates the write model; the query side serves read models (denormalized views) updated asynchronously. This lets you scale reads independently (often the dominant load) and use purpose-built read stores. CQRS is not free — it adds duplication and eventual consistency, so apply it only where read/write profiles genuinely diverge (e.g., a trading system, a reporting-heavy app).

Instead of storing "current balance = 100", Event Sourcing stores the events ("Deposited 50", "Withdrew 30", "Deposited 80"). The current state is derived by replaying events, or maintained as a projection. Benefits: a perfect audit log, the ability to reconstruct past state, and natural fit with CQRS (events drive read-model updates). Drawbacks: event schemas must evolve carefully, storage grows, and querying current state needs a projection. Snapshots mitigate replay cost.

Also called "ports & adapters", it puts the domain model at the center, completely free of framework, database, or transport concerns. The domain defines ports (interfaces it needs or offers). Adapters live on the outside and bind those ports to concrete tech (REST controller, JPA repository, Kafka listener). This makes the core testable in isolation and lets you swap infrastructure (e.g., replace PostgreSQL with DynamoDB) by writing a new adapter, not by rewriting business logic. Combined with DDD, hexagonal architecture is the backbone of maintainable, evolvable systems.

flowchart LR
    CLI["REST Adapter"] -->|command| P1["Port: Command Bus"]
    P1 --> DOM["Domain Core\n(hexagon)"]
    DOM --> P2["Port: Event Publisher"]
    P2 --> KAF["Kafka Adapter"]
    KAF --> READ["Read Model Adapter\n(projection)"]
    READ --> Q["Port: Query Bus"]
    Q --> UI["GraphQL Adapter"]

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant A as Aggregate
    participant E as Event Store
    C->>A: Deposit(50)
    A->>A: apply -> emits Deposited(50)
    A->>E: append event
    C->>A: GetBalance
    A->>E: load events
    E-->>A: Deposited(50), Withdrew(30)...
    A->>A: replay -> balance
    A-->>C: 100
